title: Extensions: mechanisms, deformation and hair, molecules

chapters.title: Rigid bodies and kinematic pairs
chapters.what: A free rigid body has six degrees of freedom: three translations and three rotations. A joint (kinematic pair) allows only some motions, the twists in its allowed subspace, and supplies reaction forces against the other 6 − f.
chapters.looks: The six freedoms as free / locked / coupled tiles (2D); the body moving by its allowed twists, with translation arrows and rotation rings, greyed when locked (3D).
chapters.change: Switch the joint: tiles lock and the body's motion narrows (▶ plays an allowed motion).
chapters.use: Hinges, drawers, vices, driveshafts, hip joints, robot arms.
misc: A joint does not remove motion by magic: it pushes back with reaction forces.
A screw joint has one freedom, not two: turning and sliding are locked together.

chapters.title: Mechanisms and mobility
chapters.what: Connect links by joints and count: the Kutzbach–Grübler formula predicts the mobility from the numbers of links and joints. It fails for special geometries, so the numerical mobility (joint variables minus the rank of the loop-closure Jacobian) is the reliable test.
chapters.looks: The kinematic diagram (2D) and the 3D model (3D), driven through a cycle by ▶.
chapters.change: Change the mechanism: most agree, but the Cardan joint, Bennett linkage and redundant parallelogram break Grübler's count.
chapters.use: Engines, pumps, robots, flight simulators, suspension, packaging machines.
misc: Grübler's formula counts, it does not check geometry.
An overconstrained mechanism can move if its dimensions are special.

chapters.title: Deformers in graphics
chapters.what: Game engines and VFX bend, twist and taper shapes with global deformations, and move characters by skinning: every vertex follows a weighted blend of bone transforms. The deformation gradient F and J = det F tell whether volume is kept or lost.
maths: \mathbf x=\varphi(\mathbf X),\quad \mathbf F=\partial\mathbf x/\partial\mathbf X,\ J=\det\mathbf F
chapters.looks: A side view of the bar's grid lines before and after (2D); the deformed bar (3D).
chapters.change: Ramp the deformer (▶); switch LBS to DQS at a bent elbow and the collapse disappears.
chapters.use: Character animation, product styling, visual effects, medical shape modelling.
misc: Linear blending of rotations is not a rotation: LBS loses volume at joints.
A bend stretches the outside and compresses the inside.

chapters.title: Hair strands
chapters.what: A hair strand is a thin rod: its shape is described by curvature κ and torsion τ along its length (a curl is a helix with constant κ and τ). Simulators keep it inextensible, either exactly (Follow-The-Leader) or through stiff constraints, and pull it back towards its rest curl.
chapters.looks: The strand's side view, rest curl dashed (2D); the strand hanging from a head (3D).
chapters.change: Tighten the curl or add wind (▶ plays the simulation); the segment lengths stay exact.
chapters.use: Film and game hair, fur, grass, cables and ropes, surgical sutures.
misc: A curl is a helix: it has torsion as well as curvature.
Stiff springs are not the only way to keep length; FTL does it geometrically.

examples.title: A curl's curvature
examples.world: Central differences on 120 particles give κ ≈ 11.54 against the exact 11.48.

examples.title: A curl's torsion

chapters.title: Molecular dynamics
chapters.what: Move every atom by Newton's law under a pair potential (Lennard-Jones) with a symplectic integrator (velocity Verlet). Temperature, pressure and structure (g(r)) come out as averages over the motion.
maths: \mathbf v_{n+\frac12}=\mathbf v_n+\tfrac{h}{2}\mathbf a_n,\ \mathbf x_{n+1}=\mathbf x_n+h\mathbf v_{n+\frac12}
chapters.looks: The particles (or g(r)) at the current time (2D); g(r) revolved about one atom, so the neighbour shells show as rings (3D).
chapters.change: Change the state: a gas of scattered atoms, a liquid with a first neighbour shell, a crystal with sharp peaks.
chapters.use: Materials design, drug binding, protein folding, lubrication, battery electrolytes.
misc: Temperature in MD is kinetic energy per degree of freedom.
g(r) peaks mark neighbour shells, not bonds.

examples.title: A Lennard-Jones gas
examples.world: Argon-like atoms at low density: the Berendsen thermostat holds T = 1.5.

chapters.title: Collision theory and reaction dynamics
chapters.what: Molecules react when they collide hard enough along their line of centres (E ≥ Eₐ) and in the right orientation (steric factor P). Averaging over the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution gives the Arrhenius law; the potential-energy surface shows the barrier as a saddle.
chapters.looks: An Arrhenius plot from sampled collisions, or contours of the H + H₂ surface with its saddle (2D); the fraction of collisions over the barrier or the surface itself (3D).
chapters.change: Raise T: the fraction above Eₐ grows exponentially; narrow the reactive cone: P and k fall.
chapters.use: Combustion, atmospheric chemistry, catalysis, drug stability, food spoilage.
misc: Activation energy is a barrier height, not the reaction's energy change.

examples.title: The collision-theory rate constant
examples.world: Trautz (1916) and Lewis (1918): k = P πd² ⟨v_rel⟩ e^{−Eₐ/kT}.

examples.title: Sampled collisions agree
examples.world: 40 000 Monte Carlo collisions reproduce the formula within about 3 %.

examples.title: The steric factor
examples.world: Only collisions inside a 30° cone react: P = (1 − cos 30°)/2 = 0.067.

examples.title: The Arrhenius plot
examples.world: ln k against 1/T is nearly a straight line of slope −Eₐ (Arrhenius 1889).

examples.title: The H + H₂ barrier
examples.world: On this LEPS surface the symmetric saddle lies 0.229 eV above H + H₂ (Karplus, Porter & Sharma 1965 used a surface of this family).

examples.title: The transition state
examples.world: At the saddle both H–H distances are equal: the activated complex of Eyring's theory.
